strengths: The paper studies an interesting and timely question: whether classical reductions between graph CO problems can guide transfer learning and multi-task pretraining for neural CO solvers. This framing is original enough to be valuable, especially compared with prior unified CO work that often chooses tasks heuristically.

The methodology is reasonably coherent: a shared GCON backbone, task-specific energy/Hamiltonian losses, and sequential decoders are applied across MIS, MVC, MaxClique, MaxCut, MDS, and coloring. The pairwise MIS/MVC and MIS/MaxClique experiments are well motivated by known reductions.

The empirical results contain useful signals: GCON with the chosen losses is competitive on individual tasks; MIS/MVC transfer benefits from head inversion and full fine-tuning; and multi-task pretraining often improves low-resource fine-tuning, especially for MaxCut and coloring.
The paper is mostly readable and explains the connection between reductions and transfer clearly at a conceptual level.
weaknesses: The central claim that computational reducibility can systematically guide transferable models is only weakly supported. Many gains are small, inconsistent, or confined to low-resource synthetic settings; MDS shows no transfer benefit in leave-one-out, MaxClique gains are marginal, and several conclusions rely on qualitative interpretation rather than controlled causal evidence.

The experimental scope is limited. Most transfer experiments use small RB or BA synthetic graphs, with little evidence on larger graphs, real-world graph distributions, out-of-distribution graph sizes, or harder benchmark suites. This substantially limits the significance of the claimed step toward foundation models for CO.

Baselines and comparisons are incomplete. The paper compares GCON variants and a few prior neural solvers, but does not sufficiently benchmark against strong classical heuristics/approximation algorithms, recent unified CO methods, or runtime-quality tradeoffs. Without this, it is hard to judge practical usefulness.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the manuscript. The abstract says an open-source implementation is provided but the URL is blank; key hyperparameters, dataset generation details, training schedules, decoder settings such as k, compute budget, and tuning procedures are not specified enough to reproduce the results reliably.

The statistical evidence is thin. Several tables report only 3 or 5 runs, significance testing is absent, and some improvements are within or close to standard deviations. The paper sometimes treats such small differences as meaningful.

There are presentation and technical consistency issues: the text refers to softmax where the model uses sigmoid, Table/experiment numbering becomes inconsistent when discussing #10-11 as #12-13, and there are typos or notation issues in the loss descriptions. These do not destroy the contribution but reduce confidence.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. The paper does not clearly discuss computational cost, failure modes of neural CO solvers, risks of overclaiming foundation-model implications, or the environmental cost of multi-task pretraining.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant question: whether computational reductions among graph combinatorial optimization problems can guide transfer learning for neural CO solvers. This is a potentially useful conceptual direction for building more general neural solvers.

The pairwise MIS/MVC/MaxClique experiments are intuitive and expose some nontrivial behavior: transfer is easier when the reduction preserves graph topology, while MaxClique transfer through the complement graph creates distribution shift. This is a reasonable empirical observation.

The work evaluates several CO tasks, including MIS, MVC, MaxClique, MaxCut, MDS, and coloring, and uses unsupervised energy/QUBO-style losses with a GCON backbone rather than relying on expensive exact labels.
Some baseline comparisons and ablations are included, such as comparing GCON against GCN/GIN/GATv2/GFN on RB-small and testing frozen versus fine-tuned transfer settings.
weaknesses: The central claim is substantially overextended. The paper presents the work as an important step toward foundation models for graph CO, but the evidence consists of small-scale experiments on RB-small and BA-small graphs with only six tasks, short fine-tuning schedules, and mostly marginal gains. This does not convincingly support the broader conclusion.

The evaluation is weak and incomplete. Results are mostly reported as final objective values with limited statistical analysis, no significance tests, no scaling study, no out-of-distribution graph-family transfer, and no comparison to strong modern multi-task neural CO baselines such as GOAL or UniCO under matched settings.

Several reported improvements are tiny or mixed. For example, leave-one-out fine-tuning barely changes MaxClique and MIS, worsens MDS, and remains far from full training for coloring. The paper nevertheless frames the results as strong evidence of general transfer between graph CO problems.

The methodology does not clearly isolate the role of computational reducibility. Many gains may be due simply to pretraining, shared graph features, longer total compute, related losses, or architecture choice. The selected pretraining set in Section 5.2 is justified post hoc from observed results rather than from a predictive reduction-based principle.

Reproducibility is poor. The abstract says an open-source implementation is provided but the URL is blank. Important details such as graph generation parameters, train/validation/test splits, optimizer settings, learning rates, model dimensions, exact GCON configuration, loss weights A and B, k-seed decoder settings, and compute budget are missing or underspecified.

The comparison to exact or classical optimization is very limited. Gurobi appears in Table 2 for only some tasks, and the paper does not provide approximation ratios, runtimes, feasibility rates before/after decoding, or a serious discussion of whether the learned solver is competitive as an optimizer rather than only as a transfer-learning demonstration.

Presentation has multiple issues that reduce confidence: table formatting is hard to read, some experiment numbering is inconsistent in the text, the open-source link is missing, and there are grammatical/typographical errors. More importantly, the paper lacks a clear limitations section.

The paper does not adequately address ethics or broader impacts. While the domain has fewer immediate human-subject concerns, the environmental cost of training, possible misuse of optimization solvers, and limitations of claims about foundation models are not discussed.

strengths: The paper asks an interesting and timely question: whether classical polynomial reductions can inform transfer and pretraining choices for neural graph combinatorial optimization. This conceptual framing is original enough to distinguish the work from standard multi-task neural CO papers.

The methodology is technically coherent: the authors use a common GCON backbone with task-specific Hamiltonian/Ising losses, sequential decoders for validity, and a clear progression from single-task baselines to pairwise transfer and multi-task fine-tuning.

The empirical results are encouraging. MIS/MVC transfer behaves as expected under complementarity, MIS-to-MaxClique experiments carefully separate frozen, fine-tuned, complement-graph, and feature settings, and the multi-task experiments show consistent low-resource fine-tuning gains for most tasks.

The paper is generally well written and candid that reducibility does not translate trivially into neural transfer. It discusses distribution shift from graph complementation and reports negative or weak cases such as MDS and frozen complement-graph transfer.
weaknesses: The evidence is still somewhat narrow for the breadth of the claims about foundation models or universal neural CO solvers. Most transfer experiments are on RB-small or BA-small graphs, with limited evidence on larger graphs, out-of-distribution graph families, or practically important benchmark suites.

The central reducibility-to-transfer claim remains suggestive rather than fully established. The experiments show correlations and useful heuristics, but do not isolate whether gains come from reducibility itself, shared loss geometry, graph statistics, task-head initialization, or generic multi-task regularization.

Comparisons to recent multi-task neural CO methods are mostly conceptual rather than empirical. The paper compares single-task GCON to several baselines, but the multi-task/fine-tuning claims would be stronger with direct comparisons against GOAL, UniCO, SAT-based representations, or generic multi-task pretraining without reduction-informed task selection.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the abstract says an open-source implementation is provided, but the URL appears blank. Important implementation details such as dataset sizes, exact hyperparameters, decoding seed counts, A/B loss weights, and compute budget are not sufficiently surfaced in the main text.

Some experimental conclusions rely on small numbers of runs and small absolute differences, especially MaxClique and MIS/MVC transfer results. Significance testing or confidence intervals over more seeds would help distinguish robust transfer from optimization noise.

Limitations and ethics are only lightly treated. There are no major ethical concerns apparent for this work, but the paper should more explicitly discuss computational cost, failure modes of approximate solvers, and risks of overclaiming optimality or generality for NP-hard tasks.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and timely question: whether classical polynomial reducibility can inform transfer learning among neural solvers for graph combinatorial optimization. The framing is original relative to much neural CO work, which often chooses pretraining tasks heuristically.

The experimental scope is reasonably broad: the manuscript covers MIS, MVC, MaxClique, MaxCut, MDS, and coloring; studies pairwise transfer and multitask pretraining; and includes additional large-graph, size-extrapolation, timing, and DIMACS zero-shot experiments.

The methodology is mostly clear. The paper specifies the GCON backbone, energy-based unsupervised objectives, task-specific decoders, datasets, and main hyperparameters, and it gives useful ablations against GCN/GIN/GATv2/GFN on RB-small graphs.

The empirical findings contain useful nuance rather than only positive results: topology-preserving MIS/MVC transfer works best, complement-graph transfer needs full fine-tuning, frozen backbones often fail under distribution shift, and explicit reduction chains can become impractical due to graph blow-up.

The appendix comparison between multitask learning and unified-task reductions is a valuable diagnostic experiment, showing that true reductions may be theoretically valid but practically harmful for GNN transfer when they induce large structural shifts.
weaknesses: The central claim that computational reducibility can guide transferable neural CO models is only partially supported. The strongest evidence is for very closely related tasks such as MIS/MVC and MIS/MaxClique, where the reductions are structurally simple; for the broader six-task setting, the task selection argument is mostly heuristic and the empirical gains are mixed.

The improvements in the multitask experiments are often small or inconsistent. In Table 5, leave-one-out fine-tuning improves MaxClique and MIS only marginally and worsens MDS. In Table 7, the proposed fine-tuned model beats 20-epoch baselines but remains worse than fully trained single-task models for several tasks, especially coloring, MaxCut, MaxClique, MIS, and MVC.

The evaluation is largely restricted to synthetic RB and BA graph families. The DIMACS experiment is only zero-shot and compares mainly against random initialization, not against strong classical or neural solvers, so it does not establish competitiveness on realistic hard instances.

The baselines are not fully convincing for the main contribution. The paper compares GCON variants and some prior solvers in Table 2, but the multitask/foundation-model claims would require stronger comparisons to recent generalist CO methods, SAT/Max-SAT representation methods, and compute-matched pretraining/fine-tuning alternatives.

Compute accounting is incomplete. Fine-tuning for 20 epochs is compared with 20-epoch and 200-epoch from-scratch training, but the pretraining cost is not incorporated into the main efficiency claims. This makes claims about rapid adaptation and resource efficiency harder to interpret.

The method is not a unified solver in a strong sense: it still relies on task-specific losses, task-specific heads, and task-specific greedy decoders. This weakens the foundation-model language and limits transfer conclusions to shared backbones rather than general task solving.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful details. The abstract says an open-source implementation is provided, but the extracted manuscript does not include an actual URL. Important details such as the A/B loss coefficients, number of decoder seeds K, exact dataset splits, random seeds, early stopping criteria, and full training schedules are not all clearly specified.

The presentation has several rough edges and overclaims: e.g. references to “foundational models” and “universal neural solver” are stronger than the evidence supports, and the impact statement is generic. There are also minor typos and inconsistencies, including duplicate mention of MDS in the loss discussion and numbering inconsistencies in the MaxClique transfer analysis.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting question: whether classical polynomial reductions can inform transfer and multitask pretraining for graph combinatorial optimization. This framing is potentially useful and not just another single-task neural CO benchmark.

The manuscript includes several empirical settings rather than a single transfer result: pairwise MIS/MVC/MaxClique transfer, leave-one-out multitask transfer, selected multitask pretraining, size extrapolation, and zero-shot DIMACS checks.

The GCON plus energy-loss baseline appears competitive among the neural baselines reported on RB-small, especially for MVC and MaxClique, and the paper gives useful implementation details for architecture, datasets, decoders, and training hyperparameters in the appendix.
The authors are appropriately cautious in places, acknowledging that reducibility and transferability are not trivially aligned and that topology-changing reductions introduce distribution shift.
weaknesses: The central claim is substantially overextended. The experiments show limited empirical transfer among a small set of synthetic graph CO tasks, but do not convincingly support the broader language about foundation models or universal neural CO solvers.

The connection between computational reducibility and neural transfer is mostly asserted rather than established. The strongest pairwise examples, MIS/MVC and MaxClique via graph complement, are very special and largely obvious; the paper does not provide a predictive theory for when reductions should induce transfer, beyond post-hoc explanations about topology and distribution shift.

The empirical evidence is weak relative to the claims. Most main experiments use only RB or BA synthetic graphs with 200-300 or 800-1200 nodes, and the DIMACS evaluation is zero-shot only, limited to MIS/MaxClique, and not competitive with specialized solvers. This leaves open whether the method transfers to realistic distributions or hard instances in a practically meaningful way.

Several reported improvements are marginal or mixed. In Table 5, MDS becomes worse after fine-tuning, MaxClique and MIS gains are tiny, and the strongest gains are concentrated in MaxCut/coloring. In Tables 7 and 11, the 200-epoch single-task full baselines often remain better, especially for coloring. These results do not justify claims such as avoiding negative transfer or learning broadly reusable CO representations.

The compute comparison is not soundly framed: fine-tuning for 20 epochs after 200 epochs of multitask pretraining is compared against training from scratch for 20 epochs, but the total training cost and amortization assumptions are not analyzed carefully. This makes the practical significance of the speedup unclear.

Baselines are insufficient for an ICML-level claim about general neural CO transfer. The paper does not compare the multitask method against recent generalist or cross-problem neural CO methods under matched settings, despite citing GOAL, UniCO, SAT-based approaches, and RL multitask solvers.

The choice of pretraining tasks appears heuristic and partly post-hoc. The selected MDS/MIS/coloring backbone is motivated by a mixture of prior reductions, leave-one-out observations, and Table 6, but there is no systematic ablation over possible task subsets or clear selection criterion.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says an open-source implementation is provided, but the URL is blank in the manuscript text. Important details such as loss weights A/B, decoder seed count k, early stopping criteria, exact dataset splits, and code for reductions are either missing or not sufficiently specified for reliable reproduction.

Presentation has several issues: table/experiment numbering is inconsistent in the MaxClique transfer discussion, there are typos and malformed equations, and some claims are rhetorically stronger than the data warrants. The impact statement is boilerplate and does not engage with possible misuse or limitations of neural optimization systems.

The limitations discussion is scattered rather than explicit. The paper notes some distribution-shift problems, but does not clearly delimit the method’s dependence on synthetic graph families, hand-designed task losses, rule-based decoders, and known task-specific reductions.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and timely question: whether classical polynomial reducibility between graph CO problems can inform neural transfer and multitask pretraining. This framing is original enough to be useful, and the manuscript is refreshingly honest that reducibility and learned transfer are related but not equivalent.

The methodology is technically sensible: energy/QUBO-style unsupervised losses, a strong GCON encoder, task-specific decoders that enforce constraints, and controlled transfer variants such as frozen backbone, full fine-tuning, inverted heads, complement-graph training, and multitask pretraining.

The empirical results provide credible evidence of useful transfer in several settings. MIS/MVC transfer is especially compelling, and the MaxClique experiments carefully separate topology-preserving from topology-changing reductions. The leave-one-out and three-task backbone studies also show practical gains over short from-scratch training for most tasks.

The paper includes useful ablations and appendices: GCON layer comparisons, reduction-based unified-task baselines, BA-small/BA-large results, size extrapolation, inference timing, and DIMACS zero-shot checks. These make the work more convincing than a purely conceptual transfer paper.
Presentation is generally clear. The paper explains the CO objectives, reductions, architecture, and transfer settings in a way that should be accessible to both graph ML and CO readers.
weaknesses: The central claim about reductions guiding foundation-model-like CO transfer is still only partially supported. The strongest evidence comes from a small set of closely related graph problems, especially MIS/MVC/MaxClique, where the reductions are unusually direct. It remains unclear how predictive reducibility is beyond these cases, or whether the observed transfer is mostly due to shared losses, shared feasible-set structure, graph distribution similarity, or decoder behavior.

The evaluation is mostly on synthetic RB and BA graph distributions, often with pretraining and fine-tuning on the same distribution. The DIMACS study is useful but limited to zero-shot MIS/MaxClique-style evaluation and is not enough to establish robust out-of-distribution transfer.

Comparisons to modern unified neural CO methods are discussed but not directly benchmarked in the main multitask setting. The paper compares against local GNNs, GFN, Gurobi in limited cases, and reduction-based alternatives in the appendix, but lacks a strong empirical comparison to recent multitask/generalist CO solvers under matched compute and tasks.

Several multitask gains are modest. MaxClique improves only marginally over the 20-epoch baseline, MDS can degrade in leave-one-out transfer, and coloring has high variance and remains far from the full-training result. This weakens the broad claim that the learned backbone reliably avoids negative transfer.

The reproducibility story is incomplete: the abstract says an open-source implementation is provided, but the URL appears blank in the manuscript. Hyperparameters and datasets are described reasonably well, but the missing code link is a material issue for a paper with many transfer settings and custom decoders.

The paper could better disentangle training-time acceleration from final solution quality. Many conclusions rely on matching or beating 20-epoch baselines, while full 200-epoch single-task models still outperform in some important cases. This is useful, but the contribution should be framed more as efficient warm-starting than as a general neural solver.

The impact statement is boilerplate and does not seriously discuss limitations or risks of using approximate CO solvers in downstream domains such as logistics or healthcare, despite those applications being mentioned in the introduction. This is not a major ethical flaw, but the treatment is thin.
